phonemes.desc: Short alpha with acute pitch plus tau — the name begins with a strained, lifted beat.
Lambda-alpha-sigma, the final syllable that bears the weight.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AT-lass' — the first syllable is pitched high, as if lifting; the second is level and heavy.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: τλάω (tláō), 'to endure, to bear, to dare' — the traditional Greek etymology

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *telh₂- 'to bear, support' — a possible root; Beekes judges the name's deeper origin uncertain

kin.label: Atlantic
kin.form: from Atlas — the sea beyond the pillars he holds; the range, the moon crater, and a star in the Pleiades all keep his name

pronunciation.note: Átlas is Tier 2 because the Greek Ἄτλας preserves stress (acute on the first alpha) but no long vowel. The name's short, heavy sound mimics the burden it describes: a single pitched syllable followed by the weight of the final syllable.

domains.title: The Bearer of Heaven
domains.subtitle: Strength, Endurance, Astronomy, and the Western Edge
domains.lead: Átlas is the Titan who holds up the sky. He is not a villain but a defeated rebel, condemned to bear the celestial sphere on his shoulders for eternity. His endurance becomes a kind of heroism: he does not triumph, but he does not collapse.

cards.name: The Celestial Sphere
cards.desc: He holds the sky aloft on its pillars, keeping heaven and earth apart so that the cosmos can exist (Homer, Odyssey 1.52-54).

cards.name: Endurance
cards.desc: His punishment is eternal labor, singled out from the Titans cast into Tartarus — forced usefulness instead of oblivion (Hesiod, Theogony 744-750).

cards.name: Astronomy
cards.desc: Diodorus makes him the first to discourse on the celestial sphere; his daughters the Hesperides tend the garden of the western sky (3.60.1-3).

cards.name: The Western Boundary
cards.desc: He stands at the edge of the known world, where the Pillars still bear his name and the sun goes down (Herodotus 4.42).

symbols.name: Celestial sphere
symbols.meaning: The heavens he supports — the Farnese Atlas marble still shows the constellations incised on it

symbols.name: Pillars
symbols.meaning: The Pillars of Herakles, once called the Pillars of Atlas — the gate of the Mediterranean at the western edge

symbols.name: Globe
symbols.meaning: Later iconographic fusion of the sky and earth, and the reason map-books are called atlases

symbols.name: Book or scroll
symbols.meaning: His astronomical knowledge — Diodorus' Atlas was a star-king as much as a load-bearer

symbols.name: Apples of the Hesperides
symbols.meaning: The golden apples guarded by his daughters, the prize that brought Herakles to his shoulders

symbols.name: Bent posture
symbols.meaning: The weight of the cosmos on his shoulders — the most copied pose of any Titan

mythology.lead: Atlas belongs to the defeated generation of gods, yet his punishment became Greece's image of endurance itself: the rebel turned load-bearer, the edge of the world where sky meets sea. His myths are few — a war, a labor, a petrification — but they carry an entire cosmography, and a name the Renaissance would place on every book of maps.

myths.title: The Sky on His Shoulders
myths.text: Atlas fought on the Titans' side in the war against the Olympians, and when the war was lost the punishments were apportioned: most rebels went down to Tartarus, but Atlas received a perpetual assignment — to hold the sky itself (Hesiod, Theogony 744-750). Homer already knows him there: in the Odyssey (1.52-54) Atlas 'knows all the depths of the sea, and holds the tall pillars which keep earth and sky apart,' a figure at the western edge of the world, near the isle where the nymph Calypso dwells. Later tradition pictures the labor as conscious, unceasing, and utterly solitary — the one punishment Zeus could not delegate to a pit. The sentence is a kind of inverted mercy: not thrown beneath the world like the other defeated, but made into its load-bearing wall. The rebel is converted into infrastructure, and the cosmos rests on his endurance whether anyone watches or not.

myths.title: Herakles and the Golden Apples
myths.text: One of Herakles' labors was to fetch the golden apples from the garden of the Hesperides — daughters of Atlas at the world's western rim (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.11). Herakles offered to hold the sky while Atlas fetched the fruit, or, in Diodorus' variant (4.26.2-3), Atlas proposed the exchange himself. The famous moment of cunning follows: Atlas returns with the apples and offers to deliver them to Eurystheus personally, clearly intending never to resume the burden; Herakles pretends to agree, asks only to be eased for a moment — 'let me put a pad on my shoulders first,' he says — and walks away. In some accounts he leaves the Pillars standing as permanent props. The myth turns brute endurance over to intelligence: the strongest mortal survives by out-thinking the strongest Titan, and the sky learns to rest on columns instead of a conscience.

myths.title: Perseus and the Gorgon's Head
myths.text: Later tradition gave Atlas a stone ending. When Perseus flew past on his way home with the Gorgon's head, he asked the Titan for rest and hospitality; Atlas, remembering an oracle that a son of Zeus would one day rob him of his golden apples, refused and tried to drive the hero off (Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.627-662; Hyginus, Fabulae 150). Perseus did not draw his sword — he turned his face away and held up the head of Medusa, and Atlas 'became a mountain; his hair and beard became woods, his shoulders and hands ridges, his head the summit.' The Atlas range of North Africa was read as his petrified body, and heaven, the poets said, still rests on its ridge-line. The myth closes his story with the very immobility he was condemned to: hospitality refused at the edge of the world becomes landscape, and the guest he turned away becomes the constellation beside him.

myths.title: Atlas the Star-King
myths.text: Greek historians tried to give Atlas a biography. Diodorus Siculus (3.60.1-3) reports that the Atlantians honored a wise king Atlas — son of a local Uranus — who was the first to discourse on the celestial sphere, 'which is why the myth,' he writes, 'shows him bearing the heavens on his shoulders'; his daughters, named Hesperides, inherited the royal garden at the world's edge. The genealogy is already Hesiodic in its confusion: the Hesperides 'with the fair golden apples' are daughters of Night in the Theogony (215), but the Hesiodic Catalogue made them Atlas's own daughters. Diodorus' rationalizing is not idle antiquarianism: it preserves the intuition that star-knowledge and world-bearing are the same metaphor — to hold the sky is to know it. The Titan's punishment and his wisdom turn out to be one image seen from two sides, and both sides point west.

lore.syncretism: The Romans kept his Greek name untranslated — there was no Latin Titan to absorb him. Renaissance cartographers placed him, sphere in arms, on the title-pages of map-books; by Mercator's time the book itself was called an atlas, so the Titan's punishment became the emblem of world-knowledge. The Farnese Atlas, a second-century CE marble in Naples, preserves the oldest surviving celestial globe with the Greek constellations in place. Modern astronomy repeats the name everywhere at once: the Atlas Mountains, the lunar crater Atlas beside the crater Hercules, a star in the Pleiades, a moon of Saturn. He has become science fiction's favorite archetype too — the being engineered to hold up a world — from Ayn Rand's Atlas Shrugged to every story that asks who carries what cannot be put down.
lore.culturalLegacy: Atlas is the West's archetype of the burden-bearer, his bent shoulders reproduced from temple metopes to corporate logos; Charles Atlas borrowed even his physique. In astronomy his name outranks the hero who freed him — the star Atlas, the lunar crater, the Saturnian moon. The word 'atlas' is now simply the word for a book of maps. Restoring Átlas restores the sound of the short, pitched first syllable under which the whole sky is held — a name that turned a cosmic sentence into the West's permanent image of quiet, sustaining strength.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Atlas is the god of the weight that does not end. He is not punished with pain but with labor — the same labor, forever. There is no transformation, no reward, no release. Yet he is not entirely pitiable. His burden is also his identity: without it, he is just another defeated Titan.

The modern world has many Atlases: caregivers, essential workers, anyone whose effort keeps the structure upright. The restoration of his name is a recognition that some forms of greatness are not dramatic but sustaining — the willingness to hold what would otherwise fall.
lore.archaeology: The Farnese Atlas in the National Archaeological Museum, Naples (inv. 6374), a Roman copy of a Hellenistic original, holds the oldest surviving celestial globe, its forty-one constellations preserving Greek star-data. The Temple of Zeus at Olympia (ca. 470-456 BCE) displayed a metope of Herakles receiving the apples from Atlas. Pausanias describes Atlas carrying the heaven on the chest of Cypselus and on votive offerings at the Heraion (5.17-19), and Theban and Attic vases show the same bent figure. Roman North Africa made the identification literal: the mountains themselves were the Titan's petrified body, and their coins sometimes say so.
